title: Episode 57: The 1893 White City: The Columbian Exposition and the Ferris Wheel
description:
The 1893 White City: The World's Columbian Exposition and the Great Ferris Wheel. How Daniel Burnham, Frederick Law Olmsted, and Nikola Tesla transformed a swampy lakeside park into a dazzling neoclassical wonderland that defined modern America. Join Rebecca and George for an immersive historical deep dive into the triumph of the 1893 Chicago World's Fair.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In May 1893, just twenty-two years after being incinerated by the Great Fire, Chicago unveiled the greatest spectacle the world had ever seen: the World's Columbian Exposition. Across six hundred acres of former swamp on the shore of Lake Michigan, master architects erected a breathtaking neoclassical dream city of gleaming white palaces, canals, and gondolas. Lit by hundreds of thousands of electric incandescent bulbs powered by Nikola Tesla's alternating current, the White City welcomed twenty-seven million visitors and introduced inventions from Cracker Jack to the colossal Ferris Wheel. George brings us the story of Chicago's shining triumph.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: ANSWERING THE EIFFEL TOWER
In the late eighteen eighties, as the four-hundredth anniversary of Christopher Columbus voyage to America approached, Congress opened bidding for a grand international exposition to showcase American industrial, artistic, and cultural supremacy to the world. Chicago fought fiercely against New York, Washington, and St. Louis, securing the fair by pledging ten million dollars in private civic bonds backed by the city wealthy meatpacking, banking, and railroad tycoons. But the psychological pressure upon the chosen host was immense: only four years earlier, the eighteen eighty-nine Paris Exposition had dazzled the globe with the soaring iron majesty of Gustave Eiffel one-thousand-foot tower. American engineers, artists, and architects were challenged to produce something equally audacious, something uniquely American that would eclipse Paris and prove that the United States had arrived as a first-rank cultural power. Chicago leading architect, Daniel Burnham, was appointed Director of Works, charged with transforming Jackson Park—a bleak, windswept swamp of shifting sand dunes, muddy marshes, and scrub oak on the shores of Lake Michigan—into a global paradise in less than three years. Burnham rallied the nation premier artistic minds, including legendary landscape architect Frederick Law Olmsted, creator of New York Central Park, and the country most elite classical architects from Boston and New York, forging a creative coalition that would redefine American urban design for generations to come. The competition between American cities had been fierce, with New York papers mocking Chicago as a crude pork-packing center incapable of high art. Burnham took the insult personally, vowing that Chicago would create a fair that would humble New York and rival Paris. He insisted on gathering the greatest American sculptors, painters, and architects, demanding that every element of the grounds embody artistic harmony and noble scale.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: DREDGING JACKSON PARK AND OLMSTED DREAM
The logistical and environmental hurdles facing Burnham and Olmsted were staggering in their complexity. Jackson Park was prone to severe seasonal flooding, with quicksand pockets that swallowed heavy steam machinery and icy winter gales coming off Lake Michigan that froze workers hands to their steel tools. Olmsted devised a visionary hydrological plan that turned the swamp into an asset: immense steam dredges carved a labyrinth of navigable lagoons, canals, and reflecting pools, using the excavated mud and sand to build solid elevated terraces for colossal exhibition buildings. At the heart of the park, Olmsted created the Wooded Island, a wild, fifteen-acre natural bird sanctuary planted with thousands of native willows, wild roses, and Japanese irises, providing a serene green refuge amidst the architectural grandeur. Burnham established a strict military construction schedule, housing twenty thousand carpenters, plasterers, and ironworkers in temporary barracks on-site. To unify the disparate buildings designed by competing architects, Burnham decreed that every monumental pavilion must adhere to a strict neoclassical Roman and Renaissance style, share a uniform cornice height of sixty feet, and be coated in gleaming white staff—a lightweight mixture of plaster of Paris, Portland cement, and hemp fibers that gave the buildings the appearance of solid, polished marble under the prairie sun. Olmsted walked the muddy grounds with his sketchbook, carefully aligning vistas so that visitors emerging from the railway depot would be struck by panoramic views of water, classical columns, and open sky. Dredging crews worked through freezing blizzards, removing over a million cubic yards of clay and sand to create smooth waterways where electric launches could glide silently among reflecting pavilions.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE COURT OF HONOR AND THE WHITE CITY
When President Grover Cleveland pressed a golden telegraph key to officially open the exposition on May first, eighteen ninety-three, the crowd of one hundred thousand spectators gasped in sheer disbelief. Before them stretched the Court of Honor, centered upon the Grand Basin with its mirror-like waters reflecting the massive Colonnade and Daniel Chester French colossal sixty-five-foot gilded statue of The Republic. The surrounding exhibition palaces—the Manufactures and Liberal Arts Building, the Machinery Hall, the Agricultural Building, and the Electricity Building—were the largest architectural structures on earth. The Manufactures Building alone covered thirty-one acres under a single iron-and-glass truss roof, capable of sheltering three hundred thousand people at once, large enough to contain the United States Capitol and the Great Pyramid of Giza. But the true magic occurred at twilight: while most American cities were still dimly illuminated by flickering gaslight and smoky oil lamps, the White City burst into brilliant radiance with over one hundred thousand incandescent lamps and towering electric searchlights that swept across the night sky, casting a surreal, celestial glow over the white facades and reflecting off the Venetian gondolas gliding through the lagoons. Inside the vast exhibition halls, more than sixty-five thousand individual exhibits from forty-seven nations displayed the wonders of the mechanical age, from mammoth Corliss steam engines and naval artillery to fine silk tapestries and diamond tiaras. The scale was so overwhelming that guidebooks warned fairgoers of Exposition fatigue, recommending three full weeks just to view the main exhibits.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: TESLA, WESTINGHOUSE, AND THE WAR OF THE CURRENTS
The brilliant illumination of the White City was the decisive battleground in the historic War of the Currents. Thomas Edison and General Electric had bid more than one million dollars to light the fair using direct current, but visionary industrialist George Westinghouse underbid them dramatically, securing the contract for five hundred thousand dollars using Nikola Tesla alternating current system. Edison was so enraged that he refused to sell General Electric incandescent bulbs to Westinghouse, hoping to derail the project. Undaunted, Westinghouse and Tesla designed and manufactured two hundred and fifty thousand patented stopper bulbs in mere months. In Machinery Hall, Westinghouse installed twelve colossal two-phase alternating current generators, each weighing seventy-five tons, creating the largest polyphase power plant in existence. When visitors saw thousands of electric lights glowing steadily without danger, and electric elevators, moving walkways, and industrial pumps operating effortlessly on AC power, the debate was settled forever: alternating current became the universal standard for electrical grids across the globe, launching the modern electrified age and securing Tesla legacy. Tesla alternating current motors powered mammoth printing presses, looms, and pumps, proving to skeptical financiers that AC power was safe, controllable, and infinitely superior for transmitting electricity across long distances. Westinghouse victory at the Chicago World's Fair broke the back of the direct-current monopoly and paved the way for the electrification of American cities and rural heartlands.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: GEORGE FERRIS AND HIS COLOSSAL WHEEL
Yet despite the architectural splendour, Daniel Burnham was plagued by a lingering concern: the fair still lacked a singular mechanical marvel to rival Paris Eiffel Tower. Enter George Washington Gale Ferris Jr., a daring thirty-three-year-old bridge builder and civil engineer from Pittsburgh. Ferris proposed an engineering audacity that critics dismissed as madness: a colossal revolving steel wheel two hundred and fifty feet in diameter, carrying thirty-six wooden passenger cars, each the size of a railroad coach and capable of holding sixty people—a total capacity of over two thousand passengers at a time. The wheel turned on a forty-five-ton forged steel axle, the largest single piece of steel forged in America up to that time, manufactured by the Bethlehem Iron Company. When the Ferris Wheel made its maiden revolution on June twenty-first, eighteen ninety-three, it became an instant international sensation. Passengers paid fifty cents for a twenty-minute ride that carried them higher than the Statue of Liberty, offering breathtaking panoramic views of Chicago, Lake Michigan, and three neighboring states, completely redeeming American engineering ingenuity. The engineering of the Ferris Wheel was a masterstroke of precision: the massive wheel was driven by two thousand-horsepower reversible steam engines geared to heavy sprocket chains. When high prairie gales howled off Lake Michigan, the wheel barely trembled, its steel tension rods flexing smoothly under load while passengers cheered from the glass-enclosed coaches high above the midway.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE MIDWAY PLAISANCE AND POP CULTURE WONDERS
While the White City offered high culture and classical grandeur, the adjacent Midway Plaisance provided exuberant popular entertainment that birthed modern American consumer culture. Conceived as a mile-long boulevard of amusements, the Midway featured authentic cultural villages from around the world, from Cairo street scenes with belly dancing sensation Little Egypt to German beer halls, Javanese musicians, and a scale replica of Blarney Castle. It was on the Midway that iconic American foods and brands made their global debuts. Visitors snacked on a new molasses-coated popcorn and peanut confection called Cracker Jack, sampled Aunt Jemima pancake mix served by Nancy Green, chewed Juicy Fruit gum, drank Pabst Blue Ribbon beer—which won its eponymous blue ribbon at the exposition—and enjoyed hamburgers, carbonated sodas, and shredded wheat for the first time. The Midway established the blueprint for the modern amusement park, influencing entertainment visionaries from Coney Island to Walt Disney, whose father Elias Disney had worked as a carpenter constructing the White City palaces. The Midway Plaisance introduced Americans to diverse world cultures, languages, and performance traditions, sparking an enduring fascination with international travel and cultural exchange. It served as a democratic melting pot where millions of common citizens could experience global sights, novel snacks, and theatrical marvels for the price of pocket change, forever altering American popular leisure.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE LEGACY OF A GILDED DREAM
By the time the exposition closed in October eighteen ninety-three, over twenty-seven million people had passed through its gates—an astonishing figure equivalent to nearly half the entire population of the United States. Though most of the temporary staff buildings were destroyed by fire or demolished shortly after the fair closed, the legacy of the White City transformed America forever. The gleaming neoclassical layout inspired the City Beautiful movement, prompting cities across the country to construct wide boulevards, public parks, monumental civic centers, and dignified public buildings, including the celebrated McMillan Plan for Washington, D.C. Today, the fair sole remaining major structure, the Palace of Fine Arts, still stands proudly on the shore of Lake Michigan, preserved as Chicago world-famous Museum of Science and Industry. The 1893 World Columbian Exposition proved that Chicago was no longer a frontier meatpacking town, but a magnificent world metropolis capable of shaping the architecture, technology, and imagination of the twentieth century. The grand neoclassical palaces of the White City permanently reshaped American civic architecture, inspiring the design of civic centers, union stations, libraries, and university campuses across the United States. Chicago proved that an industrial city could achieve noble artistic majesty, leaving an indelible imprint upon American cultural memory that endures to this day.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The 1893 White City was a breathtaking vision of classical beauty and electrical progress that defined modern America. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we brave the icy waves of Lake Superior for the tragic tale of the Edmund Fitzgerald.
